title: Sensex Surges 1.2%, Rupee Set to Rally as Oil Crashes to Two-Month Lows on Iran Deal Hopes
excerpt: All sixteen sectors in the green, Brent at $88.55, but Tehran says it has not signed anything yet — and IT stocks keep falling.
body:
Indian equity markets opened sharply higher on Friday morning, with the benchmark Sensex surging more than one per cent and the rupee set for its strongest session in weeks, after US President Donald Trump said a peace deal with Iran could be signed as early as this weekend.

The BSE Sensex jumped 1.19 per cent to 74,709 at the opening bell. The Nifty 50 rose 1.08 per cent to 23,412. All sixteen major sectors logged gains. Broader small-cap and mid-cap indices climbed 1.4 per cent and 1.3 per cent respectively — a sharp reversal after two consecutive flat sessions weighed down by Middle East escalation fears.

The trigger was unmistakable. Brent crude fell to $88.55 a barrel, its lowest in two months, after Trump called off planned strikes on Iran on Thursday and said the Strait of Hormuz would "officially open as soon as we sign."

The Rupee Bounces

Currency traders expect the rupee to open at 95.25 to 95.30 against the dollar, after settling at 95.76 on Thursday. That would mark its sharpest single-day gain since the Reserve Bank of India rolled out emergency dollar-attraction measures last week.

The rupee had been under sustained pressure for months. India imports roughly 85 per cent of its crude oil, and the Iran-driven spike in energy prices has been draining forex reserves and widening the current account deficit. The currency dropped below pre-RBI intervention levels on Thursday, effectively erasing the relief that concessional forex swaps and NRI deposit leverage had provided.

"For the rupee, the real relief will come from a deal that pushes oil durably lower and removes the risk premium embedded in crude," a Mumbai currency trader told Reuters.

Caution Beneath the Rally

Investors have reason to be wary. Trump has claimed a deal with Iran was imminent at least three times since mid-March. Each time, talks stalled. Even now, Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said Tehran had "not reached a final conclusion" and would not compromise on its red lines.

"Obviously, the key is the message coming out of Tehran," ING Bank said in a Friday research note. "We would be cautious about assuming that the extension of the ceasefire is a done deal."

Iran announced the formal "closure" of the Strait of Hormuz on Thursday — escalating from months of severe restrictions to an outright declaration — and said it would fire on any ship attempting to transit without coordination. On Friday morning, state media reported that Iranian forces had already prevented at least one tanker from passing through. The US military said commercial ships were continuing to transit.

What Felt Different This Time

The language from Washington was more specific than in previous rounds. Trump said Vice President JD Vance would attend a signing ceremony "in Europe," and that the deal had been approved by a broad coalition including Israel, Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Qatar, Turkey, and Pakistan.

Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu clarified that Israel was "not a party" to the memorandum of understanding, though he expressed appreciation for Trump's commitment to ensuring Iran cannot develop nuclear weapons.

The European Central Bank raised interest rates for the first time in nearly three years on Thursday, citing war-driven inflation. A genuine deal would remove the single biggest inflationary pressure point in the global economy.

IT Stocks: The One Sector That Kept Falling

One sector remained firmly in the red. Indian IT stocks have now fallen for seven consecutive sessions, losing more than 10.6 per cent cumulatively. The decline has been driven by fears that AI tools — particularly after Anthropic's latest product announcements — are accelerating productivity gains in software engineering, threatening the labour-cost arbitrage that underpins India's $250 billion IT services industry.

"The key concern is that productivity improvements in software engineering are occurring much faster than in non-software domains," said Sumit Pokharna of Kotak Securities.

Private banks partially offset the IT decline, rising 0.6 per cent after the RBI's concessional forex swap facility made bank stocks more attractive.

What This Means for NRIs

For the diaspora, Friday's market moves are a concentrated proxy for everything that matters: oil prices, the rupee, remittance value, and the health of India's growth story. A weaker rupee means NRI remittances buy more in India, but it also signals economic stress. A genuine Iran deal would ease inflation, strengthen the currency, and remove the fiscal pressure that has forced India to consider widening its deficit to 4.8 per cent of GDP.

Asian markets rallied four per cent broadly. European futures pointed to a 1.8 per cent open. And in the background, SpaceX's Nasdaq debut looms — the largest IPO in history. It is a day when every market is moving at once.
